title: How a bank makes money, and why it says no
summary: A bank earns a thin spread on money it borrows from depositors and can lose the whole principal when a loan fails. That asymmetry, not personality, is why lenders are paid to be cautious.
body:
A bank earns a few points a year on a loan and can lose all of it in one default. Mr Shabazz, every question a lender asks you comes from that imbalance, so learn it first and the rest of banking stops looking arbitrary.

In plain English

A bank takes deposits and pays the depositor a low rate of interest. It lends that money out at a higher rate. The difference between the two rates is called the spread, and the spread is the bank's product, the way a contractor's product is the margin between its cost and its price.

The spread is small. Suppose the bank pays depositors 2 percent and charges you 7 percent. After the cost of running branches, staff, systems and regulation, the bank may keep perhaps 2 or 3 of those 5 points as profit. Now suppose the loan defaults and the bank recovers nothing. It has lost the entire principal, which is the equivalent of decades of spread on that loan. One bad loan erases the profit on many good ones.

That is why a banker optimises for not losing rather than for earning the most. A lender's upside is capped at interest and fees. Its downside is the whole loan. Any borrower who understands that one sentence negotiates differently from one who does not.

The banker's framework: where the money comes from

Professionals describe a bank's income in a few lines, and each one shapes how it treats you.

  • Net interest margin. The spread earned across the whole loan book, after funding costs. This is most of a commercial bank's income.
  • Fees. Arrangement fees when a loan is set up, commitment or standby fees on money promised but not yet drawn, and sometimes exit fees. Fees are earned up front and carry no credit risk once paid, which is why banks like them.
  • Relationship income. Deposits held, payroll run through the bank, foreign exchange, cards, cash management. A borrower who brings this business makes the loan more profitable and better known to the bank.

The banker's framework: why caution is structural

Caution is not a mood. It is built into how the bank is measured.

  • Losses hit immediately. When a loan stops paying, the bank must set money aside against the expected loss. That charge reduces its profit in the period it happens, not years later.
  • Careers are marked by bad loans. A loan officer is rarely promoted for one excellent loan and is often remembered for one that failed. The person across the table from you is taking a personal career risk for a small institutional gain.
  • Capital is scarce. Regulators require banks to hold capital against loans, and riskier loans consume more of it. Tomorrow's lesson covers this in detail.

A worked example

Take a hypothetical bank with a book of 100 loans of US$1,000,000 each, so US$100,000,000 lent in total.

  1. It funds the book at 2 percent and lends at 7 percent, a spread of 5 percent. On US$100,000,000 that is US$5,000,000 a year of gross spread.
  2. Operating costs take 3 percent of the book, US$3,000,000 a year. Profit before losses is US$2,000,000 a year.
  3. Now two of the 100 loans default, and the bank recovers half of each after selling the security. The loss is 2 times US$500,000, which is US$1,000,000.
  4. Two defaults out of 100, only 2 percent of the book, have taken half the year's profit. Four such defaults would take all of it.

Read that from the lender's chair. A 2 percent default rate is a disaster. A borrower who promises a 25 percent project return is offering the bank nothing it can keep. A borrower who shows why the loan will be repaid is offering the only thing the bank actually sells.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is misreading what the bank is buying. If you think you are selling the bank an investment opportunity, you will pitch growth, appreciation and market momentum. The bank hears all of that as risk, because a booming market is also a market that can turn. You will leave the meeting believing it went well and receive a decline two weeks later, with no idea why.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner pitches upside. "This area is booming, values will double, the returns are excellent." None of that moves a lender, because the lender's share of the upside is fixed. What moves a lender is certainty of repayment: low loss risk, a clear source of repayment, a second way out if that fails, and a file the loan officer can defend in front of the credit committee.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, before every lender conversation, rewrite your opening in the bank's terms. Not "here is why this project is attractive" but "here is how you will be repaid, here is what happens if the first plan fails, and here is what I have already put at risk ahead of you." Treat the loan officer as a salaried professional you are asking to take a career risk, and make the yes safe for them. That one change in framing is worth more than any spreadsheet improvement you will make this year.

It also tells you where to spend effort. Work that lowers the chance of loss, such as fixing costs, securing income evidence or cleaning up title, is worth far more to a lender than work that raises your projected return. When you have limited time before a submission, spend it on the first kind.
checklist: A bank's product is the spread between what it pays depositors and what it charges borrowers.
The lender's upside is capped at interest and fees; its downside is the whole principal.
One default can erase the profit on many good loans, so banks optimise for not losing.
Fees and relationship business (deposits, payroll, accounts) make a loan more attractive to a bank.
Losses hit the bank's profit immediately, and loan officers are judged by their failures.
Pitch certainty of repayment and a second way out, not projected returns.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A friend tells you his pitch to a bank went badly even though his project shows a 30 percent return on equity and the neighbourhood is appreciating fast. What would you tell him to change?
selftest.a: Tell him the bank cannot keep any of the 30 percent; its return is fixed at interest and fees while it can lose the whole loan. A fast-rising market also reads as volatility. He should lead with how the loan is repaid from cash flow, what protects the bank if that fails (equity already spent ahead of the loan, security, guarantees), and evidence that removes cost and income uncertainty.

apply: Write a three-sentence opening for a lender meeting on any hypothetical project that mentions repayment source, second way out and your own money at risk, and does not mention projected return.
sources: Source: the course's parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Part 1 to Part 2. Bank economics and the five Cs are standard commercial-lending practice, not law. Bank capital rules come from national regulators applying the Basel framework in their own way; any specific ratio, limit or provisioning rule here is [unverified — confirm independently] against the regulator in the country of the loan.

title: The regulator inside the bank: capital, limits and bad-loan rules
summary: Regulators make banks hold capital against loans, cap how much they lend to one borrower, and force them to recognise bad loans early. Each rule changes what a bank can offer you and how fast it can say yes.
body:
A bank is not free to lend as it likes; a regulator sets how much capital each loan consumes, how much any one borrower may receive, and how quickly a troubled loan must be written down. Mr Shabazz, when a banker says "we cannot do that", it is often one of these three rules talking, not the banker.

In plain English

A bank lends mostly with depositors' money. Regulators protect those depositors by forcing the bank to keep a layer of its own money, called capital, underneath its loans. If loans go bad, the capital absorbs the loss before depositors lose anything.

Capital is expensive for a bank, because shareholders expect a return on it. So every loan has two costs to the bank: the money lent, and the slice of capital it ties up. A risky loan ties up more capital than a safe one. To be worth making, it must either earn more or be refused.

The professional framing: three rules that shape your loan

1. Risk-weighted capital

Most countries follow some version of the international Basel framework, under which loans are given risk weights. A loan secured on a completed, income-producing building usually carries a lower weight than a speculative construction loan, and both carry more than a loan to a government. The exact weights and minimum ratios are set by each national regulator [unverified — confirm independently for the country of the loan]. You do not need the numbers. You need the consequence: construction lending is capital-hungry, so banks price it higher and ration it.

2. Concentration and large-exposure limits

A bank may only lend a limited share of its capital to one borrower or one group of connected borrowers. The limit exists so that one failure cannot sink the bank. For a small or mid-sized bank, a single development loan can approach that limit quickly. When it does, the bank must either decline, take the loan to a higher approval level, or share it with another lender. The specific percentage is set in each country's banking law or regulator guidance [unverified — confirm independently]. Connected borrowers matter: your personal loans, your companies and your partners' companies may all be counted together.

3. Loan classification and provisioning

Once a loan misses payments for a set period, the bank must classify it as impaired and set aside a provision, an expected-loss charge against its profit. Modern accounting standards push banks to provision earlier, on expected rather than incurred loss [unverified — confirm the standard in force for the lender]. For you, this means a bank reacts to early warning signs, such as a late payment or a covenant breach, faster than you might expect, because waiting costs it money on its own books.

A worked example

Use a hypothetical bank with US$100,000,000 of capital and a single-borrower limit of 25 percent of capital, chosen only for illustration.

  1. The bank's largest permitted exposure to one borrower group is 25 percent of US$100,000,000, which is US$25,000,000.
  2. You ask for a US$12,000,000 construction loan. Separately, a company in which you hold a controlling share already owes the bank US$9,000,000, and your personal mortgage there is US$1,000,000.
  3. If the bank treats all three as one connected group, your total exposure becomes US$12,000,000 plus US$9,000,000 plus US$1,000,000, which is US$22,000,000.
  4. That is 88 percent of the bank's limit for one group. Even though the new loan alone looks comfortable, it will need senior approval, and the bank may ask to share it with another lender.

The lesson is that a bank's answer depends on its whole relationship with you, not on the one file in front of it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating regulatory constraints as negotiating positions. You can argue with a banker's view of your rents. You cannot argue the bank out of its capital rules or its exposure limit. Spending a meeting pushing against a hard limit burns goodwill and time. When you hear "that would put us over our limit", the productive response is to ask what structure would fit: a smaller hold with a second lender, a longer timeline, or a different asset as security.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes every bank of a given size will say the same thing. In fact two banks with similar balance sheets can answer very differently because one is near its limit for construction lending, or for a sector, or for your borrower group, and the other is not. A decline from one bank is information about that bank's book as much as about your project. Ask, politely, whether a decline is about the deal or about the bank's appetite this year.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, before approaching a lender, list every existing facility you and anyone connected to you holds with that bank. Ask the relationship manager early whether a loan of your size is within their normal hold, or whether they would expect to syndicate or share it. Match the size of your request to the size of the bank: a large request to a small bank forces it up the approval chain and invites a no. And when a loan is underway, report early and accurately, because a bank that learns of a problem late has already had to provision for it, and will be less forgiving.

Professional sign-off required: a banking lawyer in the country of the loan, if any question turns on the actual legal limit or classification rule.
checklist: Capital is the bank's own money under its loans, and riskier loans consume more of it.
Construction loans are capital-hungry, which is why they are priced higher and rationed.
Single-borrower and connected-group limits cap how much one bank can lend you in total.
Your personal loans, companies and partners may be counted together as one exposure.
Missed payments force the bank to classify and provision, hitting its profit quickly.
Regulatory limits are not negotiable; ask what structure fits inside them instead.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A mid-sized bank tells you it likes your project but cannot lend the full amount 'because of exposure'. What has probably happened, and what two options would you raise?
selftest.a: The loan, combined with any existing loans to you or connected parties, probably pushes the bank near its single-borrower or connected-group limit. Options: ask whether it would hold part of the loan and bring in a second lender to share it, or reduce the request (with more equity or a smaller first phase) so the exposure fits inside the limit or within a lower approval level.

apply: List every loan, guarantee or account that you and any company you control hold with one bank, and total the exposure as a bank would see it.

title: Who actually decides: the relationship manager, credit risk and the committee
summary: Your relationship manager does not approve your loan; a credit committee you will never meet does, from a memo the relationship manager writes. Your real audience is that memo.
body:
The person you meet at the bank is your advocate, not your approver; the decision is made by a credit committee that reads a memo about you. Mr Shabazz, if you write your package so that memo is easy to write, you have done more for your loan than any meeting can.

In plain English

Most banks split lending into two sides. The relationship manager, often called the RM, finds and looks after borrowers. They want deals, because they are measured on the business they bring in. The credit risk side exists to say no to bad deals. They are measured on losses avoided. The two sides are designed to disagree.

Between them sits a credit committee, a group of senior people who approve, change or decline loans. You will usually never meet them. What they see is the credit memo: the RM's written case for your loan, challenged and annotated by credit risk. Whatever is not in the memo, for practical purposes, does not exist.

The professional framing: the approval path

The sequence is broadly the same at most commercial banks, though names vary.

  1. Informal conversation. The RM tests whether your deal fits the bank's appetite: the asset type, location, size and your profile.
  2. Application package. You deliver financial statements, project documents, appraisal, budget and model.
  3. Credit memo and risk rating. The RM writes the memo and proposes a risk rating. Credit risk challenges both.
  4. Credit committee decision. Approve, approve with conditions, or decline. Large or unusual loans may go to a higher committee or to the board.
  5. Commitment letter or term sheet. The approved terms, including conditions precedent, which are things that must be true before money moves.
  6. Documentation and security. Lawyers draft the loan agreement and security documents, security is registered, and only then is the first drawdown made.

The professional framing: what a credit memo contains

A typical memo covers the borrower and sponsor, the purpose and amount, the sources and uses of funds, the repayment source and the financial tests, the security and guarantees, the key risks and how each is mitigated, and the RM's recommendation with proposed conditions. Credit risk adds its own view of each risk. The committee is reading for one thing above all: has every serious risk been named and answered?

The professional framing: the risk rating

Alongside the memo, most banks give each loan an internal risk rating, a grade on a scale that reflects the chance of default and the expected loss if it happens. The rating drives the price, the capital the loan consumes, how often it is reviewed and which committee may approve it. A better rating can mean a lower margin and a faster approval. You rarely see the rating, but you influence it directly: equity paid in, cost certainty, income evidence and strong security all push it toward the safer end. When an RM asks for one more document, it is often to move the rating by a notch.

A worked example

Consider two hypothetical borrowers asking the same bank for a US$2,000,000 construction loan.

Borrower A sends a 60-page bundle: scanned documents, a spreadsheet with hidden tabs, and a covering email. The RM spends three weeks extracting the cost total, finding that the land value is unsupported, chasing a missing tax return and asking what happens if costs overrun. Each round trip takes a week. The memo is still unwritten after six weeks, and the RM moves to an easier deal.

Borrower B sends a 12-page package with a one-page summary: asset, total cost US$3,000,000, loan US$2,000,000, equity US$1,000,000 already spent, repayment from rents, coverage of 1.35 times at full rent and 1.22 times with rent 10 percent lower. A one-page risks table names completion, lease-up, cash flow and exit risk, with the answer to each. The RM lifts whole paragraphs into the memo in an afternoon.

The underlying projects may be equally good. Borrower B's loan gets to committee; Borrower A's does not. That is not unfair. It is how a busy institution allocates attention.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is that a risk you did not mention is found by credit risk instead. When a reviewer discovers a problem you left out, such as an unregistered title, an expired approval or a related-party contract, the committee stops asking how to fix that problem and starts asking what else you did not tell them. Trust, once dented in a memo, rarely recovers in the same file.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats a friendly RM meeting as approval. The RM's enthusiasm is real and also irrelevant to the final decision; they are paid to be enthusiastic. Nothing is approved until a signed commitment letter exists, and even then money only moves when the conditions precedent are satisfied. Do not commit to a contractor, a purchase or an investor deadline on the strength of "they loved it".

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, write every package as if you were writing the memo yourself. Open with a one-page summary in the bank's order: who, what, how much, repaid from what, secured by what. Include your own risks table, naming each risk before credit risk does, with the evidence that closes it. Keep numbers consistent across every document, because a mismatch between the summary and the model is the first thing a reviewer finds. Ask your RM directly: "What will credit risk push back on, and what would you like from me to answer it?" Then answer it before it is asked. Your goal is a file the RM can defend in a room you are not in.

This is the same discipline as a well-written construction submittal: the reviewer should be able to approve it without phoning you.
checklist: The relationship manager is your advocate; the credit committee decides.
Credit risk staff are paid to challenge; expect them to disagree with the RM.
The credit memo is your real audience; what is not in it does not exist.
Approval path: conversation, package, memo and rating, committee, commitment letter, documents and security, first draw.
Name every serious risk and its answer before credit risk finds it.
A friendly meeting is not approval; only a signed commitment letter with conditions met moves money.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your RM says your deal 'looks great' and asks for the package. Two weeks after you send it, she asks why the land value in your summary differs from the appraisal. What does this tell you, and what should you do?
selftest.a: It tells you credit risk, or the RM preparing the memo, is reconciling your numbers and found an inconsistency, which damages trust in the whole file. Correct it immediately in writing, explain the source of each figure, check every other number across the package for the same problem, and resend a single consistent version so the memo can rely on it.

apply: Draft a one-page summary for a hypothetical US$2,000,000 loan in the order a credit memo uses: borrower, purpose, amount, sources and uses, repayment source, security, key risks.

title: The five Cs: the universal underwriting lens
summary: Lenders everywhere judge a borrower by character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. Knowing the strongest evidence for each lets you build a file that answers the questions before they are asked.
body:
Almost every lender in the world sorts its questions into five headings: character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. Mr Shabazz, if your package has strong evidence under each of the five, you have answered most of a credit committee's questions before the meeting.

In plain English

The five Cs are a checklist that loan officers have used for generations. They are not law and not a formula. They are a way of making sure nothing important is skipped. Each C is a question, and each question has evidence that answers it well and evidence that answers it badly.

The professional framing: the five questions

Character

The question: will this person honour obligations when it hurts? The evidence: credit history, references from past lenders, contractors and partners, a track record of finishing what you start, and, often underrated, how you handle questions. A borrower who answers difficult questions directly and admits what is unknown scores higher than one who is evasive or oversells.

Capacity

The question: can the project's own cash flow repay the debt with room to spare? The evidence: a defensible operating forecast, the debt service coverage ratio on that forecast, and proof of demand such as leases, pre-sales or market studies. Week 3 covers the ratios in detail.

Capital

The question: how much of your own money is at risk ahead of ours? The evidence: cash equity actually paid in, and land contributed at a value the bank accepts. Capital matters twice. It absorbs early losses, and it proves conviction, because people are careful with their own money.

Collateral

The question: if the cash flow fails, what can we sell? The evidence: a registered first mortgage on the property, a credible appraisal, insurance with the bank named, and clean title. Collateral is the second way out, and no lender wants to rely on it. They want to know it is there.

Conditions

The question: do the market, the currency, the law and the economy support this loan? The evidence: rent comparisons, demand studies, approvals in writing, and an analysis of currency risk if income and debt are in different currencies.

The professional framing: how the Cs connect

The five Cs are not independent. Capital strengthens capacity, because more equity means a smaller loan and lower payments. Collateral depends on conditions, because a building in a weak market is worth less on a forced sale. Character colours everything, because a committee that doubts your candour will discount every figure you supply. A good package therefore does not just answer each C; it shows how strength in one shores up another. When you add equity, say what it does to coverage. When you show demand evidence, say what it does to the appraisal.

A worked example

Score a hypothetical borrower on a five-point scale for each C, the way an RM might informally.

  1. Character, 4 of 5. Clean credit history and good references, but no previous development completed.
  2. Capacity, 3 of 5. Coverage of 1.30 times at full forecast rent, falling to 1.17 times if rent comes in 10 percent lower, below a typical minimum of 1.20 times.
  3. Capital, 4 of 5. US$400,000 cash already spent on design and approvals, plus land the bank appraises at US$300,000, against a total cost of US$2,000,000. That is US$700,000 of equity, 35 percent of cost.
  4. Collateral, 5 of 5. Clean registered title in the borrowing company's name, as-complete appraisal of US$2,600,000.
  5. Conditions, 3 of 5. Good rent comparisons, but no signed leases, and rents in a different currency from the loan.

The total is 19 of 25, but the useful reading is not the total. It is the two weakest Cs, capacity and conditions, which are where the committee will press. The fix is visible: a signed pre-lease or two would lift both capacity and conditions at once, and matching the loan currency to the rent currency would remove the currency question.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a single fatal C hidden behind four strong ones. Excellent collateral does not rescue a loan whose cash flow cannot pay the debt, because a bank that has to sell your building has already failed at its job. A strong sponsor does not rescue unregistered title, because the bank cannot take security over land you do not legally own. Lenders tend to decline on the weakest C, not average across all five.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner leans on collateral: "Even if it goes wrong, the land is worth more than the loan." To a lender, that sentence is an admission that you are thinking about failure as an acceptable route. Selling security is slow, expensive and uncertain, and it damages the lender's reputation. Collateral supports a yes. It never creates one.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, build your package as five sections, one per C, and put your strongest single piece of evidence first in each. Then score yourself honestly as above and spend your remaining preparation time on the lowest two scores, because that is where the committee will spend its time. For a first project, character is answered partly by the team you hire: an experienced contractor, an independent cost consultant and a professional property manager lend you a track record you do not yet have. Write their names and experience into the character section.

A useful habit from your operations background applies here: treat each C like a pre-start checklist item that must be closed with evidence, not with a statement. "Demand is strong" is a statement. "Three signed letters of intent at the forecast rent" is evidence.
checklist: Character: will you honour obligations when it hurts? Track record, references, candour.
Capacity: can the project's cash flow repay with room? Coverage ratio on a defensible forecast.
Capital: how much of your own money is ahead of the bank? Paid-in cash and land at accepted value.
Collateral: what can the bank sell? Registered first mortgage, appraisal, insurance.
Conditions: do market, currency and law support the loan? Comparables, approvals, currency analysis.
Banks decline on the weakest C; fix the lowest two scores first.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A borrower has a superb site worth twice the loan, a modest income forecast that just meets the coverage minimum at full rent, and no leases. Which C will the committee press on, and why will the land value not save the loan?
selftest.a: Capacity and conditions. The cash flow has no headroom and the income is unproven. Land value only answers collateral, the second way out; a bank does not want to lend on the expectation of selling security, which is slow, costly and uncertain. The borrower needs income evidence or a smaller loan so coverage has headroom.

apply: Score a hypothetical project of your own design on each of the five Cs out of 5, and write one piece of evidence that would raise the lowest score.

title: Week 1 review: how banks think
summary: Six questions on bank economics, regulation, the approval path and the five Cs. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.
body:
This week was about the lender's chair: why a bank is cautious, what limits it, who decides, and how it sorts its questions. Mr Shabazz, answer each question aloud in under a minute before you read the answer.

Question 1. Why does a bank care more about certainty of repayment than about the profit your project will make?

Answer. Because the bank's return is capped at interest and fees, while its potential loss is the entire principal. The spread on a loan is a few points a year, so one default can erase the profit on many good loans. A bank therefore optimises for not losing. Your project's profit is yours, not the bank's; what the bank needs is evidence that it will be repaid from cash flow, with a second way out if that fails. Lead every conversation with repayment, not return.

Question 2. Name the three regulatory forces inside a bank that most affect a development loan, and what each one means for you.

Answer. First, risk-weighted capital: construction loans consume more capital, so they cost more and are rationed. Second, concentration or large-exposure limits: a bank can lend only a limited share of its capital to one borrower or connected group, so your total relationship can cap a new loan. Third, loan classification and provisioning: once a loan shows trouble the bank must charge expected losses against its profit, so it reacts quickly to early warning signs. The specific ratios and limits are set by each country's regulator and must be confirmed independently.

Question 3. Who approves your loan, and what document do they decide from?

Answer. A credit committee, usually people you never meet, decides from the credit memo that your relationship manager writes and that credit risk challenges. The RM is your advocate; credit risk is the sceptic; the committee is the judge. Your real audience is the memo, so write your package so the RM can lift paragraphs straight into it, with a one-page summary and a risks table that names each risk and its answer.

Question 4. List the six steps from first conversation to first drawdown.

Answer. One, informal conversation to test appetite. Two, application package. Three, credit memo and risk rating. Four, committee decision: approve, approve with conditions, or decline. Five, commitment letter or term sheet setting terms and conditions precedent. Six, legal documentation and security registration, then the first drawdown once conditions precedent are met. Nothing before step five is an approval, and no money moves before step six.

Question 5. Name the five Cs and the single strongest evidence for each.

Answer. Character: track record and references, and candid handling of questions. Capacity: a coverage ratio comfortably above the minimum on a defensible forecast, with income evidence. Capital: cash equity actually paid in, plus land at a value the bank accepts. Collateral: a registered first mortgage supported by a credible appraisal and insurance. Conditions: market comparables, written approvals and a currency analysis where income and debt differ.

Question 6. A first-time developer scores well on four Cs but has no completed projects. How does she answer character?

Answer. She rents a track record. She hires an experienced contractor on a fixed-price or guaranteed-maximum contract, an independent cost consultant, an owner's representative or project manager with completed buildings, and a professional property manager. She names them and their experience in the package. Banks underwrite the team, not only the principal, and she adds candour, references from past business dealings and a clean credit history.

Recap

A bank sells safety, not opportunity. Its caution is structural: thin spreads, immediate losses, scarce capital and careers marked by failures. Regulation sets hard limits you cannot argue with but can structure around, for example by sharing a loan or reducing its size. The decision is made by a committee reading a memo, so your package must make that memo easy and must name every risk before someone else does. The five Cs are the lens: build your file in five sections, find your two weakest, and spend your effort there.

Three habits carry forward from this week into every later lesson. First, translate everything into the lender's language: risk removed, repayment source, second way out, and your money at risk. Second, assume that every document you send will be read by a sceptic who is looking for the inconsistency, and make it consistent before it leaves you. Third, treat a decline as data. A no from one bank tells you something about its book, its limits or your weakest C, and each of those has a different fix. None of them is solved by sending the same package to more banks.

It is also worth holding on to the proportions from Monday's example. On a book where the spread after costs is about 2 percent, a 2 percent loss rate is enough to wipe out half a year's profit. When a banker seems to be worrying about a small risk, that arithmetic is why. Your task is never to argue that the risk is small; it is to show what removes it, and who bears it if it happens anyway.

Mr Shabazz, a fair test of this week is whether you could sit in the relationship manager's chair and explain to a colleague why a strong-looking project was declined. If you can name the weak C, the regulatory limit or the missing memo evidence that caused it, you have the lens. Next week moves from the bank to the building: the four risks a construction lender prices, what tips a yes, the types of loan you will meet, and how a construction loan is actually paid out.
checklist: Bank return is capped; bank loss is the whole loan.
Capital weights, exposure limits and provisioning shape what a bank can offer.
The committee decides from the credit memo; write for the memo.
Nothing is approved until a signed commitment letter, and no money moves until conditions precedent are met.
Five Cs: character, capacity, capital, collateral, conditions.
A first-time sponsor rents a track record through the team they hire.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Your relationship manager says the committee 'had concerns about the sponsor' and declined. You have strong equity and good collateral. What two things would you check first?
selftest.a: First, which of the five Cs was weakest: probably character (no track record or a credit issue) or capacity (thin coverage). Ask the RM directly which concern was decisive. Second, whether the decline reflects the bank's appetite or exposure limits rather than the deal. Then strengthen the weak C, for example by adding an experienced contractor and project manager to the team, before approaching another lender.

apply: Without notes, explain aloud in two minutes why a bank is cautious, using the spread, the loss on default and the credit memo.
